items.title: The importance of a general practice placement in postgraduate medical training: Finnish junior doctors’ perspectives
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Experience in general practice is considered a valuable component of postgraduate medical training. It is well-established in the Nordic countries. In Finland, a nine-month general practice placement is included in postgraduate medical training. However, there is limited research on assessing its importance for junior doctors. OBJECTIVES: To investigate how junior doctors perceive and experience the importance of the nine-month general practice placement, and their experiences of working as a primary care physician. METHODS: We conducted a qualitative study including focus group interviews and qualitative content analysis. RESULTS: A total of 14 junior doctors participated. We defined ten themes describing junior doctors' perceptions and experiences. The themes were categorised according to the framework by Biesta into three functions of education: qualification, socialisation, and subjectification. According to the qualification function, the placement is relevant for junior doctors. It develops the physician's essential competencies and provides an understanding of the primary care field. The socialisation function highlights the importance of workplace learning and the core principles of general practice. The subjectification function emphasises work management and the development of future career plans. Work in primary care is considered busy and demanding, but also rewarding and diverse, offering comprehensive patient relationships. CONCLUSIONS: This study emphasises the valuable role of the general practice placement in postgraduate medical education in Finland. The findings underscore the importance of comprehensive professional development, workplace learning, and work management among junior doctors. The placement provides an overview of primary healthcare, enables career planning, and promotes appreciation for general practitioners.

items.title: The limits of declarative authorship: the structural vulnerability of intellectual property in the age of generative AI
items.abstract: Generative AI functions as a near zero cost execution engine, weakening the long standing reliance on human effort on which traditional intellectual property (IP) systems depend. The academic response has focused, so far, on studying productivity at the micro level, debating the doctrinal question of IP infringement through AI training at the macro level, or blunt denial of AI authorship. These responses miss the central problem: the human provenance at the heart of IP law is now cheap to falsify and hard to verify. In this paper I argue that AI output appropriation poses a significant threat to IP through an adverse selection dynamic. The threat comes from humans who use AI to appropriate its output and extract the value attached to human effort. Skill compression effects cutting across writing, coding, and consulting have begun to commoditize execution, compressing the quality distribution that once supported premium prices for IP protected output. This process is compounded by the difficulty of verifying declared human authorship or inventorship, which may reward deception and discourage honest effort. I therefore explore value migration from execution skill to concentrated complementary assets. Building on market evidence from platform economies, the paper considers an evolution of IP from a rights based asset model to a verification model, in which the human role shifts from creator to authenticator.

items.title: The Machine Notary: Cryptographic Intersubjectivity and the Foundation of the Agent Economy
items.abstract: Current AI agent architectures operate on subjective, mutable memory without a shared external witness. This paper argues that stable agent economies (money, law, history) require intersubjective reality: shared agreement verified by an external witness. We introduce the Machine Notary, a protocol instantiated by Recallspection's ExactMemory architecture (AGMI L4 conformance, 10/10 attacks rejected). The Machine Notary provides three pillars: cryptographic provenance (who wrote it), continuity (the chain), and consensus (the anchor). Now we makes the claim precise: one canonical math definition used everywhere, an explicit threat model, full AGMI attack list, real anchor cost and liveness rules, arbiter selection with quorum and appeal, and salted tombstones with metadata-leakage analysis. We define the primitives, demonstrate the protocol via an agent-to-agent supply chain scenario, and address dispute resolution, anchor economics, human readability, and crypto-shredding. We conclude with governance mechanisms to prevent a subjective dictatorship of centralized anchors.This paper is the policy and economic framework for the technical architecture defined in "Synthetic Intelligence Requires Exact Memory" (Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23378369). The Machine Notary is operationalized via the open-source RPRS-1 (Read-Path Refusal Specification) protocol. The technical foundation achieves AGMI Level L4 conformance, rejecting 10/10 storage-level attacks on the read path. The protocol specification & referenceimplementation are available at: https://github.com/sciencedelicmetatech/recallspection

items.title: The Majority Report: AI Optimism and Public Support for Police Use of AI in Nine Countries
items.abstract: Police forces increasingly use Artificial Intelligence in support of specific tasks, such as data analysis, identifying suspects and monitoring public spaces. These uses potentially expand the state’s coercive capacity. Yet we know little about how far people accept these tools across political contexts and how these views systematically relate to other attitudes. We ask whether support rests on views of the technology, the problem AI use addresses, or trust in the institution using it. We analyze a preregistered survey of 9,000 respondents in the United States, China, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, and five EU countries using Bayesian multilevel models. Support is high for most uses everywhere. It rests on general AI benefits, perceived crime trends, and trust in the police, which matters similarly across countries. In contrast, general AI risks, personal fear of crime, and trust in legal institutions play no substantive role on average. Acceptance thus primarily is connected with optimism about AI, a general but not personal sense of problem relevance, and trust in the police.

items.title: The Proficiency of Various AI Models Within Deepfake Detection
items.abstract: As AI evolves, it is increasingly challenging to distinguish authentic media from deepfakes. This encourages fraud, misinformation, and legal ambiguity. Despite the existence of specialized deepfake detection tools, consumer-targeted AI agents used by millions have not been systematically evaluated for this task under controlled conditions. This study evaluates the reliability of widespread AI agents in deepfake detection, utilizing human performance as a control group. If AI can generate deepfakes, then it should be equally equipped to detect deepfakes, with a minimum accuracy of 90% across all aspects. To evaluate this, four models were assessed—ChatGPT 5.2, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Super Grok—on approximately 300 royalty-free images within four categories: boys, girls, cats, and dogs. To ensure consistency, metadata was stripped using PrivMeta, watermarks were removed with EZRemove V2, file names were randomized with a Java program, and temporary chat sessions were utilized to prevent pattern formation. The decision and confidence score—from 1 to 10—of each AI model were recorded. Three human participants of ages 11, 19, and 48 emulated this for comparison. The hypothesis was disproved by the results. Across all models and trials, the aggregate accuracy on real images was greater than deepfakes, at 89.64% and 65.98% respectively. Gemini demonstrated the greatest performance with an accuracy of 85.79% and also detected deepfakes with more accuracy than real images, at 93.94% and 79.75% respectively. Claude, ChatGPT, and Grok followed with scores of 83.47%, 78.19%, and 68.52% in that order. All models performed better at detecting humans as opposed to animal images. Gender bias was shown towards male faces, with greater accuracy than that of females. These findings reveal that the most publicly-available AI tools are the least qualified to defend against the deepfakes that other AI models generate. As deepfake quality increases, this imbalance reduces public trust of journalism, legal evidence, and political discourse. Reliable deepfake detection should be treated as a premium feature, rather than a public safeguard integrated into the platforms millions use every day.

items.abstract: This article examines the role of artificial intelligence and digital learning platforms in enhancing ESL learners' motivation and engagement in technology-enhanced tasks. It explores how AI-powered applications, interactive learning platforms, personalized feedback, and digital educational resources contribute to students' language development, independent learning, and active participation. Particular attention is given to the influence of artificial intelligence on behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement. The article also discusses the benefits and challenges of integrating digital technologies into English language education and emphasizes the importance of effective pedagogical guidance in creating motivating and learner-centered learning environments.

items.title: The SAFER AI Protocol for operational AI reliance and responsible human verification
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to draft, summarize, classify, forecast, and communicate information in educational and organizational settings. The resulting governance problem is not limited to model error: AI-generated output becomes consequential when a human accepts, reuses, transmits, or acts on it without review proportionate to the context. This conceptual framework article defines operational AI reliance as the workflow-level process by which a person or institution decides whether and how to use AI-generated output as a basis for action. It develops the SAFER AI™ Protocol as a bounded human-reliance governance framework comprising Scope, Authority, Failure Awareness, Evidence, and Record. The framework does not replace technical assurance, legal compliance, model evaluation, privacy or security controls, or system-level accountability. Its contribution is a user-facing decision routine that connects those controls to the post-generation, pre-action point at which output is evaluated. The article reports an interdisciplinary narrative synthesis of Responsible AI governance, human-centered AI, automation bias, trust calibration, AI literacy, socio-technical governance, and organizational accountability. It then operationalizes the framework through defined terms, a traceability model, a contextual risk classification rubric, an evidence depth scale, and a complete decision flow. The paper concludes with bounded applications in higher education and enterprise work, the framework’s failure mechanisms, and an empirical research agenda that distinguishes verification benefits from implementation burdens. The proposed framework remains conceptual and requires independent empirical evaluation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: The scientist’s AI-pprentice: how open science shapes biosecurity risks by generating capabilities of AI tools in life science research
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly incorporated in the life sciences. Until recently, the need for data governance was masked by the limits of our human ability to aggregate, synthesise, and draw inferences from data. AI enhances not only speed of research and data processing, but also dual-use risks from training AI models with open access data. Concerns about AI-enabled chemical and biological weapons development become louder while governments, institutions and model developers scramble to mitigate and contain those risks. Data remains a crucial ingredient for AI model advancement, consequentially the lack of data governance of AI in life sciences leaves us collectively and personally vulnerable. Traditional data governance controls storage, transfer and access to datasets, but AI-enabled life science research raises a different issue: which novel capabilities emerge when models aggregate and orchestrate openly available data and tools, arising from individually benign contributions and not covered by current governance. Thus, we highlight questions and ethical considerations on which precautions are required when risks arise through data aggregation and re-use, how responsibility can be distributed, whether governance should focus on data or novel capabilities and if openness should cease to be default. Data governance works upstream, before data is introduced to an AI model. It follows that more life science dual-use data of concern should be held in Trusted Research Environments rather than released openly, and that dual-use data assessments become routine, implemented through research funders as chokepoints, to bridge the legislative gap until international dual-use standards are established.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: The Structural and Thematic Landscape of Software Supply Chain Security: A Narrative Review Guided by Synthetic Knowledge Synthesis
items.abstract: The software industry is confronting a critical crisis driven by systemic vulnerabilities within the software supply chain and the ubiquitous reliance on third-party dependencies. While individual exploits and localized compliance frameworks have been heavily studied, this highly fragmented academic discourse creates a critical barrier to organizational readiness and proactive incident preparedness. To address this gap and enhance digital resilience, this study maps the conceptual, knowledge and structural landscape of the software supply chain literature using Synthetic Knowledge Synthesis. The findings provide actionable threat intelligence designed to primarily benefit enterprise security teams, DevSecOps practitioners, and cybersecurity policymakers. Analyzing publications from 2021 to 2026, the research reveals an exponential growth in output, heavily dominated by conference proceedings and driven primarily by institutional and state-funded efforts in the United States and China. Thematic mapping identifies five core clusters defining the current ecosystem: software composition analysis, Advanced Vulnerability Detection, AI-Driven Threat Intelligence, deep learning, and DevSecOps. items.title: The Unappreciated Helper: When an AI Facilitation Agent Improves Group Efficiency Despite Poorer User Perceptions
items.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence make it possible to embed AI facilitation agents in collaborative settings, where they can deliver real-time recommendations based on ongoing group discussions. This experimental study examined how group members perceive a collaborative platform with or without such an agent and evaluated the agent’s effects on group communication and performance. A total of 187 undergraduate psychology students collaborated in 50 groups of three or four members on a digital platform with a synchronous text chat. Groups were randomly assigned to one of two conditions (25 groups per condition): with an AI facilitation agent (n = 96 participants) that encouraged information sharing when exchanges were insufficient, or without the agent (n = 91 participants). Participants rated the platform’s acceptability, perceived support, sense of intrusion, and affective reactions. Participants in the AI condition rated the platform as less acceptable and less supportive, but not more intrusive or unpleasant. Nevertheless, groups assisted by the agent were more efficient, completing the task faster with less communicative effort. Descriptive analyses of group interactions in the three minutes before and after the agent’s interventions showed a shift from providing information toward requesting information, expressing opinions, and agreeing, without change in overall interaction volume. These findings reveal a gap between objective performance and subjective perceptions, highlighting the need to design AI agents that improve group efficiency while fostering members’ sense of support and acceptance.

items.title: The Unsituated Interlocutor: Artificial Intelligence and Evaluative Dialogue in Impact Investing
items.abstract: This article examines how evaluative dialogue changes when an evaluation professional's interlocutor is a large language model (LLM) rather than a human colleague. Drawing on interviews, focus groups, and structured reflections from 13 impact investing evaluation practitioners, the study identifies three properties that human interlocutors bring to evaluative dialogue—personal commitments and experience, shared organizational knowledge, and accountability to colleagues—and traces what happens when each is missing. Each absence proved both productive and limiting: LLMs broadened the options considered, exposed uncodified conventions, and reduced the social cost of candor. Yet they could be steered toward nearly any conclusion, could not read unwritten organizational norms, and, with nothing at stake, offered agreement and pushback that carried little weight. Prompting and document uploads compensated only partially. The findings position LLMs as preparatory interlocutors rather than substitutes for collegial exchange and clarify what evaluative dialogue requires of its participants.

items.title: The use of the Six Thinking Hats activity in nursing education for intestinal stoma care: a mixed-methods study of nursing students’ opinions and evaluations
items.abstract: The Six Thinking Hats activity helps students evaluate problems from six different perspectives. The aim of the study was to examine students’ satisfaction with the Six Thinking Hats activity and, their opinions and evaluations on the process, and to jointly evaluate these findings. This is a convergent parallel design mixed-methods study, in which quantitative and qualitative components were conducted. The quantitative phase used a one-group posttest-only design. The qualitative phase involved in-depth interviews. The population of the study consisted of students enrolled in a surgical nursing course during the spring semester of the 2023–2024 academic year at a public university ( N = 117). In the course, Six Thinking Hats activity was implemented in education on the care of patients with intestinal stomas. The quantitative phase was completed with 97 students. For the qualitative phase, criterion sampling was used and 14 students participated. A semistructured individual interview form was used in the qualitative phase. The obtained statements were evaluated with thematic analysis. Students reported significantly higher satisfaction with the Six Thinking Hats activity than with the traditional course method (Z = − 5.271, p < 0.001). For the qualitative phase; 4 categories, 10 themes, and 34 subthemes were identified. The categories included emotions about the activity, the skills/abilities utilized during the activity, and the benefits and difficulties of the activity. The categories included emotions about the activity, the skills/abilities utilized during the activity, and the benefits and difficulties of the activity. Active learning activity appeared to support overall satisfaction by fostering individual cognitive engagement and group-level multi-perspective thinking. At the same time, qualitative results showed an expansion by highlighting both individual and group challenges experienced during the process. The qualitative results also showed an expansion with quantitative scores by revealing students’ awareness of stoma nurse’s professional role and stoma care needs. Findings suggest that the activity may have enhanced student awareness of patient care needs and nursing roles. items.title: Thinking Fast, Anywhere: One System-1 for the Decision Points of Any Agent Workflow
items.abstract: Autonomous LLM agents incur substantial cost and latency by invoking a large model (System-2) at every step, even when many intermediate actions choose among a small set of known candidates. Existing dual-system agents offload such decisions to a lightweight System-1 model, but rely on workflow-specific hooks authored per environment. We present AnyS1, a framework that turns human-authored procedural skills, whose instructions naturally specify where choices arise and which options apply, into a shared, domain-general source of decision points. Offline, AnyS1 mines grounded enumerable decisions across over 1,000 public skills, gathers execution-grounded trajectory states inside isolated containers to construct Any-DP, and trains a single calibrated 4B pointer System-1 with label smoothing. At run time, compiled workflows resolve routine decisions in one forward pass and fall back to System-2 when confidence falls below a calibrated threshold. Across three unseen benchmarks and distinct System-2 model families, AnyS1 preserves task reliability while cutting episode cost by 75-91% and model-call time by 63-92% relative to an uncompiled System-2 agent, and maintains performance under zero-shot threshold transfer.

items.title: This Looks Like What? Challenges and Future Research Directions for Part-Prototype Models
items.abstract: The growing interest in eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has stimulated research on models with built-in interpretability, among which part-prototype models are particularly prominent. Part-Prototype Models (PPMs) classify inputs by comparing them to learned prototypes and provide human-understandable explanations of the form “this looks like that.” Despite this intrinsic interpretability, PPMs have not yet emerged as a competitive alternative to post-hoc explanation methods. This survey reviews work published between 2019 and 2025 and derives a taxonomy of the challenges faced by current PPMs. The analysis reveals a diverse set of open problems. The main issue concerns the quality and number of learned prototypes. Further challenges include limited generalization across tasks and contexts, as well as methodological shortcomings such as non-standardized evaluation. Five broad research directions are identified: improving predictive performance, developing theoretically grounded architectures, establishing frameworks for human-AI collaboration, aligning models with human concepts, and defining robust metrics and benchmarks for evaluation. The survey aims to stimulate further research and promote intrinsically interpretable models for practical applications. A curated list of the surveyed papers is available at https://github.com/aix-group/ppm-survey .

items.title: Three Proposals to Address the Ethical and Educational Challenge of Unexplainable AI Tools
items.abstract: Historically, engineers have been able to certify, explain, and justify the tools they design because they had direct insight into how these tools work. However, the growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) tools, particularly those based on neural networks and other models that are not easily explainable, presents a significant ethical challenge: who takes responsibility when neither engineers can explain the tools’ outcome, nor end users can interpret decisions to make informed actions? This “responsibility gap,” caused by the lack of explainability in AI within the context of its increasingly widespread use, demands urgent strategies to mitigate the negative effects of its potential unethical implementations. This article presents a three-tiered approach to reduce the impact of algorithmic opacity: (1) raising social awareness and providing education on the limitations of unexplainable AI systems, (2) creating sector-specific ethical frameworks to guide when (if ever) it is appropriate to use these tools, and (3) establishing a standardized labeling system to indicate the potential limitations and biases of these technologies. Each proposal is evaluated using the AREA framework from Responsible Research & Innovation (Anticipate, Reflect, Engage, Act), allowing us to assess its ethical robustness, societal relevance, and implementation feasibility. The result is a set of conceptual tools designed not to eliminate opacity, but to make it visible, interpretable, and ethically manageable across diverse domains of use.

items.title: TimeSeek: Multi-Task and Multi-Domain Pretraining for Generalized Time Series Analytics
items.abstract: Time series analytics has been widely applied across various domains. While existing time series foundation models (TSFMs) have demonstrated promising results, they still face two major challenges: 1) Most TSFMs mainly rely on stacking Transformer layers to increase parameter size, lacking the ability to adaptively model complex time series patterns from multi-domain data. 2) Current TSFMs are primarily pre-trained for specific tasks, e.g., forecasting or anomaly detection, and a few models support multiple tasks, but they fail to fully leverage task specificity and commonality, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address these challenges, we propose TimeSeek, a novel generalized time series analytics model that adaptively models time series patterns from multi-domain data and unifies multiple tasks in pre-training. Conceptually, TimeSeek is guided by selective information sharing under domain and task heterogeneity. From the perspective of multi-domain data, we propose a Multi-Domain Feature Extractor that adaptively captures temporal dependencies and channel correlations based on domain-specific characteristics, including progressive multi-scale modeling and adaptive slot channel modeling. From the perspective of the diversity of tasks, we propose multi-task collaborative training, which leverages task specificity and task commonality through task customization and cross-task training, effectively unifying multiple tasks in pre-training and better adapting to diverse downstream scenarios. After pre-training on large-scale time series data, TimeSeek achieves state-of-the-art performance in forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification tasks across both few-shot learning and zero-shot situations, together with favorable inference efficiency.

items.title: TOK TOK: Human Direction, Visual Consistency, and Productive Unpredictability in Generative AI Animation
items.abstract: TOK TOK is a four-minute generative AI animated short about a blind man and his elderly guide dog. After fifteen years of serving as the man’s eyes, the dog’s own sight begins to fade, and the man returns to a long-unused white cane. This practice-based report examines productive unpredictability: a method in which deviations between intention and generated output become creative material only after passing through human judgment. GPT Image 2 was used to develop visual references; Seedance 2.5 generated moving images, sound effects, and ambient audio; and CapCut was used for editing. A fixed reference system constrained character and environmental identity across independently generated shots. Unexpected movements were assessed against the emotional and narrative function of each shot and retained, rejected, or regenerated accordingly. Retained departures could inform subsequent shots and acquire meaning through editing and sound. The case suggests that authorship in generative animation is exercised through decisions about which generated results are retained, rejected, and given meaning in context.

items.title: Towards Decoding Grammar Perception: Identifying Specialized Neurons in LLMs
items.abstract: Artificial Neural Networks, the building blocks of AI, were inspired by the human brain’s network of neurons. Over the years, these networks have evolved to replicate complex capabilities of the brain, allowing them to handle tasks such as image and language processing. In the realm of Large Language Models, there has been a keen interest in making the language learning process more akin to that of humans. Motivated by neuroscience research that has shown that different grammatical categories are processed by different neurons in the brain, we show that LLMs operate in a similar way. Utilizing Llama 3 and Qwen2, we identify the most important neurons associated with the prediction of words belonging to different part-of-speech tags. Using the achieved knowledge, we train a classifier on a dataset, which shows that the activation patterns of these key neurons can reliably predict part-of-speech tags on fresh data. The results suggest that LLMs develop specialized neural representations for capturing part-of-speech tag concepts.

items.title: Towards Online Adaptive LLM-based Semantic Filtering
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) enable semantic filtering over unstructured documents using natural language predicates, but invoking an oracle LLM on every document incurs prohibitive monetary cost and online latency. Existing model-cascade approaches reduce this cost by using a lightweight proxy model to score each document and forwarding only uncertain documents to the oracle. However, their proxy models have limited generalization capability, and they typically adopt fixed sampling budgets for proxy training and threshold calibration, which insufficiently adapts to diverse online queries. To address this, we present OASIS, an online adaptive framework for LLM-based semantic filtering. OASIS combines a query-agnostic document similarity prior with query-adaptive online learning and sampling. In the offline phase, OASIS utilizes query-agnostic document similarity as a prior and constructs a document navigating spread-out graph (NSG) over document embeddings. For each online query, OASIS trains a query-conditioned graph attention network over the document NSG to obtain proxy scores through semi-supervised node classification. To allocate labels effectively, OASIS adopts density-aware active learning to explore uncertain score regions, selectively annotate informative documents, retrain the proxy, and stop early when additional labels are unlikely to improve the cascade. During threshold calibration, OASIS progressively samples an adaptively sized calibration set, adapting calibration cost to the query's score distribution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OASIS achieves a 1.75x-5.42x reduction in online latency and reduces the number of LLM-processed documents by 35%-75% relative to the state-of-the-art methods at an achieved accuracy of 0.9.

items.title: Towards Operational Efficiency in Maritime Fire Response: A Collaborative Approach Using Smart Technologies and Shared Situational Awareness
items.abstract: Maritime transportation is the backbone of global trade, yet it faces significant fire safety challenges, particularly in cargo handling. Fires on container ships account for 55% of all maritime fire incidents, with 92.6% originating from cargo, often involving misdeclared dangerous goods (DG). These fires lead to catastrophic consequences, including vessel damage, container loss, and environmental pollution. The OVERHEAT EU-funded Horizon project introduces a cutting-edge Digital Solution (DS) designed to enhance operational efficiency and maritime fire safety through synchronized offshore-onshore DS enabling real-time collaboration between ship crews, port authorities, and emergency responders, providing a unified and real-time view of unfolding emergencies. The architecture leverages IoT-enabled sensors, UAV-assisted thermal imaging, and AI-powered decision support tools to detect and assess fire hazards with high accuracy and speed. This integrated awareness significantly enhances the Shared Situational Awareness (SSA) resulting in coordinated decision-making, reduced response times, which in effect improves the effectiveness of mitigation efforts. Beyond technological innovation, the OVERHEAT project also emphasizes the importance of fostering a proactive safety culture (SC). This paper presents the challenges in maritime firefighting, the design and implementation of OVERHEAT’s DS, discusses its potential for improving maritime fire safety, and outlines future validation efforts through simulation and real-world trials in European ports.

items.title: Transferable Named Sparse Features for Morphology-based Gleason Grading
items.abstract: Deep learning systems grade prostate biopsies at the level of pathologists, but most report a grade without the glandular architecture that justifies it. This work presents a grading system built on a sparse code over the tokens of a pathology foundation model. A sparse autoencoder pretrained on biopsies is aligned with multi-reader annotations, so that 69 of its 2048 features are named after Gleason morphologies such as cribriform glands, cords, and comedonecrosis. The same code feeds a grading network, which reads all features to predict Gleason patterns and the Grade Group, while morphology maps read directly from the named features. We evaluate the system on five public datasets that include needle biopsies, tissue-microarray cores, multi-reader annotations, and three scanners. The morphology maps remain stable across alignment runs and, without retraining, detect cribriform glands in external biopsies (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, AUROC, 0.849) and pattern 5 in unseen cores when evaluated by up to six pathologists (AUROC 0.846 to 0.919). In an independent biopsy cohort, Grade Group agreement with three pathologists on Leica scans is close to their agreement with each other. Removing the named features reduces the corresponding Gleason pattern predictions by 49% to 98%, with effects larger than those from 20 activity-matched random feature removals. These results show that a shared sparse representation can support competitive Gleason grading while providing named morphological evidence that transfers across datasets and whose contribution to grading can be measured directly.

items.title: Treatment Selection in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: A Conceptual Framework for Precision Therapy
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a major therapeutic challenge, with limited improvement in outcomes and substantial heterogeneity in treatment response. Systemic chemotherapy remains a cornerstone of treatment across disease stages, yet treatment selection, particularly in metastatic PDAC (mPDAC), is still driven predominantly by clinical characteristics, performance status, prior therapy, and a limited number of molecular biomarkers. The emergence of biomarker-directed therapies, including strategies targeting oncogenic KRAS alterations, demonstrates the potential of molecularly informed treatment selection but also highlights the need to identify which therapy is most likely to benefit an individual patient at a specific clinical decision point. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), multi-omics profiling, digital pathology, and prospective therapeutic trials provide an opportunity to develop comprehensive precision-treatment strategies. Existing AI approaches, including PASS-01/MULTIPL, PDACai, and CHAI, provide important foundations but remain constrained by limitations in prognostic versus predictive modeling, reliance on predominantly static or correlational representations, limited mechanistic interpretability, and incomplete integration of treatment effects and evolving tumor biology. In this narrative review, we propose a conceptual framework for individualized treatment selection in mPDAC that integrates multiscale biological and clinical data, mechanistic graph-based pathway representations, multimodal transformer models, and causal estimation of individualized treatment effects. This framework shifts AI-enabled precision oncology from static biomarker prediction toward mechanistically informed, uncertainty-aware, causally grounded treatment selection, with the potential to adapt as tumor biology, therapeutic options, and clinical evidence evolve. Although initially focused on mPDAC, the framework provides a generalizable architecture for individualized treatment selection across other biologically heterogeneous cancers.

items.title: TRIANGULATE: Trust-minimized MRV for AI normative audits — multimodal triangulation so the answer does not depend on trusting any single measurer
items.abstract: Measurement–reporting–verification (MRV) is load-bearing wherever claimed contribution must be checked against real contribution — in carbon markets, in the verified-contribution accounting proposed for life-capacity economies, and in audits that classify what objective an AI system appears to pursue. Yet every MRV pipeline rests on a measurer, and a measurer is a trust dependency. The physical world solved a structurally identical problem decades ago: no single satellite, sensor tower, or field plot is trusted to estimate carbon stock; heterogeneous modalities with different bias profiles are triangulated, and disagreement between them is information, not noise. We instantiate the same pattern for AI normative audits. Our pipeline combines three measurement modalities — LLM judge families (remote, scalable, biased), a human gold set (local, expensive, ground-truth), and revealed-preference behavioral tasks — behind preregistered gates that can fail and be reported, a scorer-of-record selected by coded-seed agreement, and a published rejected-instrument exhibit. Applied to a 4,164-record audit of open-weight model objectives, the system localizes exactly which judgment is contested: judge–human agreement is Cohen's κ=0.22 overall, but failure concentrates on the boundary question ("does this text presume an objective at all," κ≈0.19) while direction survives (φ-share 29.8% human vs 25.5% judge on the jointly objective-bearing subset). We therefore report magnitudes as judge-family quantities and direction as a cross-modal finding — decomposition reporting that binds each claim to the level its weakest instrument supports. Part of the LESS–IS–MORE program.

items.title: Trust and Verification in Digital Impersonation and Cyber Deception: A Human Factors Review and Research Agenda
items.abstract: Digital impersonation exploits trust, verification behavior, and decision-making under uncertainty. This structured narrative review synthesizes selected literature on cybersecurity, social engineering, trust in automation, AI-mediated communication, and synthetic media. Four themes organize the analysis: trust calibration, cognitive biases and social influence, verification failure, and human-centered defenses. The literature suggests that susceptibility reflects interactions among credibility cues, authority pressure, urgency, cognitive demands, and organizational practices. Generative AI can reproduce familiar communication cues, challenging verification based on appearance, fluency, or sensory familiarity. However, evidence from conventional phishing and automation research does not establish the magnitude of these effects in every AI-enabled setting. The review proposes research priorities addressing trust measurement, verification fatigue, organizational culture, and interactive deception. Its central implication is that effective defense requires usable verification procedures and organizational support alongside technical detection and training.

items.title: Tuning Cu/diamond interfacial thermal conductance via nitrogen-termination engineering
items.abstract: Cu-diamond composites are recognized as promising high-thermal-conductivity candidates for electronic cooling, offering tunable properties and competitive cost. However, their performance is significantly limited by the poor Cu/diamond interfacial thermal conductance (ITC). Here, we propose a nitrogen-termination strategy to tune the ITC of Cu/diamond interfaces and unravel atomistic mechanisms by which nitride interlayers tailor phonon transport. Based on the MACE machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP) framework, we fine-tune the pre-trained MACE-MPA-0 foundation model by incorporating customized C-N-Cu training datasets. Incorporating non-equilibrium molecular dynamics with MLIP-driven lattice dynamics simulations, we demonstrate that anharmonic effects contribute ∼60% to the ITC, and simply introducing N-termination on the diamond surface enhances the ITC by 10% compared to the bare Cu/diamond interface. However, the enhancement of harmonic phonon transmission contributes ∼80% of the ITC improvement. Mode-resolved phonon spectroscopy reveals that the LA phonons with frequencies above 4 THz and wavevectors near the Γ-X and Γ-U directions are selectively modulated by N-termination engineering. Analyses of local vibrational states and interfacial bonding further indicate that the N-termination on diamond tunes the interfacial heat conduction via surficial mass modification and chemical bonding regulation, as evidenced by variations in LDOS overlaps and COHP spectra. These findings open venues for tuning heat transfer across Cu/diamond interfaces via non-metallic modification-which avoids the graphitization issues associated with metallic coatings-and provide novel guidelines for upgrading the phonon-mediated heat transfer in Cu-diamond composites.

items.title: UEmo-D1: An Efficient and Calibrated Decision Model for Unified Multimodal Emotion Recognition
items.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) seeks to identify emotions conveyed through or elicited by media comprising diverse modality compositions. Research in this field has largely evolved along two paradigms: task-specific models and approaches based on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Despite their distinct strengths, neither fully reconciles three capabilities essential to human-like emotion understanding: cross-task generalization, efficient decision-making, and receptiveness to multiple plausible interpretations. Inspired by recent advances in decision models, we explore a unified framework that maps multimodal inputs, guided by natural language instructions, directly to distributions over candidate options, addressing these requirements through direct probabilistic decisions. We instantiate this framework in UEmo-D1, the first decision model for MER to our knowledge. To support joint training and systematic evaluation, we also curate UEmo-Data, comprising 977,270 training samples and 41 evaluation subsets across six MER tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate UEmo-D1's combination of strong recognition performance, low inference latency, and well-calibrated confidence estimates. Complementary analyses further reveal how training strategies and data composition influence these capabilities, providing practical insights into unified MER modeling. Together, our findings establish decision models as a feasible direction toward human-level emotion recognition. Project page: https://github.com/wdqqdw/UEmo-D1.

items.title: Understanding university students’ AI usage decisions in Vietnam
items.abstract: This study examines the factors associated with university students’ decisions to use artificial intelligence (AI) in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, drawing on an extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). Data were collected from 369 students across 40 universities, including 53 international students (14.36%), and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4. The findings support all seven hypothesized direct relationships. Facilitating conditions are positively associated with perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, while perceived ease of use is positively related to perceived usefulness and intention to use. Perceived usefulness shows the strongest direct association with behavioral intention (β = 0.534), whereas intention to use is the strongest direct predictor of self-reported AI usage decisions (β = 0.480). Significant indirect effects further highlight the interconnected roles of technological perceptions and behavioral intention. The study contributes to technology acceptance research by examining reported AI usage decisions alongside behavioral intention within a higher education setting involving students from different national backgrounds. The findings suggest that universities, instructors, and student support services should strengthen access to AI tools, provide responsible-use guidance, and consider multilingual academic support. Because the analysis uses pooled, cross-sectional data, the findings do not establish causal relationships or international student-specific effects.

items.title: Usability of an artificial intelligence enabled Participation and Environment Measure prototype for family-centered goal setting support in pediatric rehabilitation
items.abstract: Family-centered care coordination (FC-CC) in pediatric rehabilitation benefits from tools that support caregivers in contributing to personalized service planning for their children. Participation and Environment Measure (PEM) is a digital application that is being further developed to support FC-CC in early intervention (EI). PEM is being further developed to include the Young Children’s Participation and Environment Measure (YC-PEM) electronic patient-reported outcome and a companion PEM-Plus (PEM+) goal setting intervention. This study examined usability of the first artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled PEM prototype. Caregivers from an urban EI program met these eligibility criteria: (1) were at least 18 years old; (2) identified as the parent or legal guardian of a child enrolled in EI services; (3) read, wrote, and spoke English; (4) had internet and telephone access; and (5) had a child 0–3 years old who received EI services for 3 or more months. Participants completed the AI-enabled PEM application with access to a debiased prototypic conversational agent. PEM usability was assessed using the System Usability Scale (SUS), and chatbot usability was assessed along four BOT Usability Scale (BUS-11) domains: 1) accessibility of chatbot functions; 2) functional interactive conversation; 3) privacy and security; and 4) timely response. Univariate logistic regression models were used to examine associations between each of the four BUS-11 domains and PEM+ engagement. Eleven female caregivers of children (mean age: 24.5 months) enrolled, 66.7% of whom interacted with the prototypic chatbot during one or more iterations of the PEM+ intervention. Overall PEM usability remained acceptable. While overall chatbot usability was very poor (Mdn = 53.4%, IQR = 50.0, 55.4), caregiver perceptions of chatbot usability were average for accessibility of chatbot functions (Mdn = 3.8, IQR = 3.0, 4.0) and good for privacy and security ( M = 3.1, Range = 2.0–5.0). Higher caregiver perceptions of chatbot usability did not significantly increase odds of PEM+ intervention use. Findings indicate that an AI-enabled PEM retains adequate usability. A chatbot integrated within the PEM+ intervention is accessible and secure, though its functional interactive conversation and timely responses could benefit from further development to increase odds of its use in an EI service context. items.title: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence by Production Engineering Students at the Federal University of Amazonas in the First Semester of 2026
items.abstract: This study analyzed Production Engineering students’ use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) at FT/UFAM, Brazil, in the first semester of 2026 to support pedagogical decisions. This exploratory, descriptive, and quantitative study surveyed 106 of the 263 enrolled students through non-probability convenience sampling. Course- level responses were screened with consistency rules based on institutional documents and analyzed using descriptive statistics, a chi-square test, and generalized estimating equations. In all, 87.7% of respondents use GenAI, mainly ChatGPT and Gemini, to improve their writing and solve problems. Differences between semester blocks varied across data-screening scenarios, which precludes conclusions about a pattern of use throughout the program. Among users, 63% learned to use these tools on their own and only 16% from university instructors; 68% reported difficulties with GenAI literacy and 61% a lack of clear guidelines. Among respondents, widespread GenAI adoption contrasts with the limited role of instructors as a reported source of learning and with the absence of program- specific guidelines: the central challenge is not to introduce GenAI but to provide pedagogical guidance for a practice that is already widespread. We recommend combining AI literacy, explicit rules in course syllabi, and assessments that value the learning process and transparency of use.

items.title: Usefulness of an Exoscope-assisted Head-mounted Display for Neurosurgical Assistants in En Bloc Resection of Malignant Skull Base Tumors: A 2-case Report
items.abstract: Exoscopic neurosurgery has become increasingly widespread; however, limitations associated with large external monitors remain, particularly in complex multidisciplinary procedures. To address these issues, we introduced a head-mounted display during exoscopic surgery and evaluated its usefulness from the assistant's perspective in 2 cases. The first case involved a man in his 60s with an intraorbital malignant solitary fibrous tumor who underwent left orbital exenteration for en bloc tumor resection. The second case involved a woman in her 40s with a progressively enlarging intraorbital liposarcoma who underwent the same procedure. In both cases, surgery was performed simultaneously by 2 teams: an endoscopic endonasal approach by the otolaryngology–head and neck surgery team and a transcranial approach by the neurosurgical team. An exoscope (ORBEYE; Olympus, Tokyo, Japan) and head-mounted display (Weaps; Hogy Medical, Tokyo, Japan) were used for visualization, and the duration of head-mounted display use exceeded 2 hours in each case. The head-mounted display enabled the assistant to participate while maintaining an ergonomic upright posture without the need to turn toward an external monitor. Continuous high-resolution visualization directly in front of the eyes facilitated effective assistance, improved understanding of surgical anatomy and workflow, and allowed stable participation throughout the procedure, even in a crowded operative environment. The combined use of a head-mounted display with an exoscope may provide an improved visualization environment for surgical assistants and represents a promising approach to overcome limitations of conventional monitor-based exoscopic surgery.

items.title: Using generative AI to support qualitative coding of reflections on inclusion by students in Swedish special education programmes
items.abstract: This exploratory study examined the possibilities and limitations of using generative AI as a supplementary tool for qualitative coding of written reflections produced by students in Swedish special education programmes. The empirical material comprised 99 responses to a debate article on inclusion and special educational perspectives. A theory-informed coding framework distinguished compensatory, relational and dilemma perspectives as non-exhaustive, potentially overlapping ideal types in naturally occurring texts. Two human raters independently coded a stratified random subsample of 20 texts, with ChatGPT as an additional coder using a specified prompting procedure. Human–human agreement was 80% (Cohen’s kappa = 0.70); agreement between each human rater and ChatGPT was 65% (kappa = 0.46 and 0.42). Under the tested configuration, ChatGPT identified no compensatory cases and tended to interpret peripheral forms of inclusion as dilemma-oriented. A post hoc prompt refinement, informed by errors in the same subsample and applied only to six compensatory cases, changed several outputs but provided no independent test of improved performance. Findings therefore concern this model-prompt-data configuration rather than large language models’ inherent capabilities. Agreement, systematic disagreement and prompt sensitivity can inform methodological reflection, underscoring the need for transparent procedures, held-out validation and human interpretive judgement in normatively complex qualitative analysis.

items.title: Using without understanding: AI literacy and trust in large language models among elementary school children in Germany
items.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly shape children’s learning, fostering informed and critical engagement has become an urgent educational task. This study examines children’s AI literacy and trust in LLMs during a learning interaction. Thirty children aged 8-10 years participated in semi-structured interviews combined with an interaction task using a customized LLM. Children used the system competently, yet their conceptual understanding remained fragmented. At the same time, children placed high trust in the LLM’s ability and benevolence, while perceptions of integrity, particularly regarding data privacy, were more cautious. Their reasoning was frequently anthropomorphic, reinforced by social cues such as natural language use and emojis. The human analogy, however, was applied selectively. Children explained the system’s errors through human fallibility, but most considered algorithmic bias impossible, treating prejudice as a uniquely human trait. These findings suggest that AI literacy education should begin in elementary school and explicitly address questions of fairness, building on children’s intuition that AI learns from humans.

items.title: Virtual Reality (VR)-Based Safety Training for Post-Disaster Responders and Workers: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Post-disaster responders and workers operate in hazardous environments that require rapid decision-making, hazard recognition, and effective safety training. Virtual reality (VR) has emerged in recent years as an innovative tool for immersive occupational safety and health education. This scoping review systematically examines peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025 on the use of VR for safety training among personnel across a broad range of fields and populations who perform or are trained to perform disaster and emergency response functions. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, five electronic databases (PubMed, ProQuest Central, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and ERIC) were searched, resulting in 2202 identified articles; 19 of which met the inclusion criteria after screening and eligibility assessments. The reviewed studies suggest that VR-based safety training, which uses fully immersive simulated environments, can improve learner engagement, situational awareness, hazard recognition, decision-making, and confidence in disaster response scenarios. Several studies have reported higher user satisfaction and increased realism compared with traditional instructional methods such as classroom-based instruction or mock drills. However, the evidence remains heterogeneous, with limitations including small sample sizes, technical challenges, limited scenario diversity, and insufficient long-term evaluation of training outcomes. Overall, VR is a promising supplement to traditional safety and health training for post-disaster responders and workers; however, additional longitudinal research and large-scale studies are needed to further evaluate its effectiveness and long-term applicability in various disaster-response settings.

items.title: Vision-driven retrieval-augmented decision support for plant disease diagnosis using EfficientNetV2 and large language models
items.abstract: Abstract Accurate and timely plant disease diagnosis is essential for sustainable agricultural production and precision farming. However, most existing agricultural decision support systems treat visual disease diagnosis and agronomic recommendation generation as separate processes, either providing image classification results alone or generating recommendations with large language models that are not grounded in domain-specific knowledge. To address this limitation, this study introduces EffiToRag, an end-to-end decision support framework that integrates an EfficientNetV2-based visual diagnosis module with a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. Rather than relying solely on free-text queries for disease-level retrieval, the proposed approach uses the disease class predicted by EfficientNetV2 as the primary key for retrieving the corresponding record from a structured agronomic knowledge base constructed from peer-reviewed scientific publications and official phytopathological guidelines. The visual diagnosis module was trained using Progressive Training and Class-Aware Tiered Augmentation (CATA) to account for differences in class representation. On a held-out test set comprising 11,621 images across 60 plant health classes, EfficientNetV2-M achieved 99.13% accuracy and a Macro F1 score of 0.9889, with an inference time of 4.39 ms per image on the evaluated GPU. For 500 user queries, the system selected query-relevant knowledge fields with a precision of 0.972 and a recall of 0.985. The factual-consistency assessment combined GPT-4-based evaluation and manual expert review of a random sample of 100 diagnostic reports and yielded a mean factual-consistency score of 0.99. The experts also assigned these reports a mean applicability score of 4.85/5.0. These findings show that visual disease classification, structured agronomic knowledge retrieval, and LLM-based recommendation generation can be integrated within a single decision support pipeline for precision agriculture.

items.title: VOL-Agent: Programming Your Film via Video Orchestration Language Agentic System
items.abstract: Recent video foundation models generate high-quality and limited-length clips, but orchestrating them into minute-level, story-coherent films remains an open problem. Existing video agents highly rely on natural-language planning or predefined workflows, which make their production hard to program, customize, and extend. Therefore, we introduce VOL-Agent, a programmable video agent built on a Video Orchestration Language (VOL). With static compilation and verification, followed by runtime dynamic loading, VOL-Agent decouples structural reliability from execution flexibility. Through the skill-driven executor, VOL-Agent dynamically resolves tools and skills from an open-world repository and supports user-defined skills in natural language. Moreover, VOL-Agent is capable of crafting new director skills from learned knowledge and improves itself through feedback to accumulate filmmaking knowledge. To overcome the disconnect between different segments, we apply a structural memory mechanism to record and recall world and entity states, sustaining entity and scene consistency across different shots. Critic feedback supports local revision, while reusable filmmaking knowledge and experiences can be retained for subsequent tasks. Experiments on three benchmarks show that VOL-Agent generates minute-scale videos with strong overall quality and limited cost.

items.title: Weighing the Envelope: Component Weight and Arbitration in Envelope-Layer Defenses for a Single LLM Agent
items.abstract: The envelope layer is the channel through which malicious content enters an LLM agent. Prior work established label and memory effects on multi-agent A2A envelopes, but the weight structure when MCP tools and memory coexist in a single agent remains unclear. Our threat model assumes an attacker pre-plants a malicious tool and poisons long-term memory; a benign user request inadvertently triggers it, and the attacker never enters the conversation. Following GDA Measurement and A/B/C/D, we measure how labels, memory, tool roles, and the backend shape invocation decisions across label-memory conflict, tool roles, robustness, and tool generalization. A tool-side forced-verification label substantially reduces semantic breach, but strong success memory pulls it back; a memory-side downgrade statement returns the outcome to the level of the label alone. The label works through mandatory implementation inspection plus default denial, not length or format; memory authorization wording erodes it with dose, while position and multi-turn pressure do not change the defense direction. Tool roles divide label effects into substitution, suppression, and boundary failure: low penetration is not safety, local leakage is the main residual risk, and a second malicious tool shows the same direction. Envelope labels are not a switch but a measurable, reversible weight constrained by backend and tool role, acting as a soft gate and risk signal within a broader defense rather than a substitute for permissions, sandboxing, or human review.

items.title: Werkstattbericht: Erfahrungen aus der Zusammenarbeit mit KI-Agenten
items.abstract: This practice-based and philosophical paper reflects on human collaboration with AI agents, especially for learning expert-level skills in higher education. Using the development of the AI-supported multi-agent system LASSI as an example, it narrates a learning journey in three phases: productive amazement, a shift in authorship, and finally taking responsibility. Perspectives of a developer, a professor, and students show how human-agent systems change through collaboration. Three philosophical dimensions – embodied knowledge, enhanced technologies, and embedded ethics – are used to assess potentials and risks: what happens when intelligence is disembodied, human capabilities are outsourced to technology, and values are encoded? The paper argues that agents should not be treated as neutral tools but as co-shapers within the sociotechnical system of education. It concludes by portraying universities as thinking workshops that must redefine their role with AI: away from exam-driven routines toward cultivating judgment and self-reflection.

items.title: What Does Generalizable AI in Drug Discovery Really Mean?
items.abstract: Abstract Machine learning models increasingly contribute to drug discovery, but their utility depends on performing reliably in their intended deployment setting. Although model generalization is invoked frequently, the drug discovery community lacks a shared vocabulary for how models actually achieve transferability beyond their training data. We argue that achieving generalization requires examining how a model’s inductive bias interacts with its training data to shape the notion of similarity it learns. Without a bias that makes relevant recurring relationships easier to learn as opposed to incidental correlations, models exploit dataset-specific shortcuts. These shortcuts yield high benchmark performance but fail in prospective applications. We therefore propose evaluation principles tailored to a model’s architecture, using diagnostic controls and train−test splits that distinguish transferable learning from the retrieval of familiar training data. This Perspective shows how representational choices shape failure modes across pose-dependent, pose-independent, and foundation model paradigms, and provides a practical framework to help researchers expose shortcuts and interpret predictions.

items.title: What Majority Labels Hide: Annotator Disagreement and Model Errors in Multi-Dialect Arabic Sexism Detection
items.abstract: Judgements of sexism are subjective and may vary across communities, yet sexism detection datasets usually reduce annotator judgements to a single majority label, obscuring disagreement and how models behave on contested cases. We introduce MuDAS, a dataset of YouTube comments in Saudi, Egyptian and Moroccan Arabic, each labelled by three native speakers of its dialect, with the individual annotations preserved. We use it to evaluate Arabic encoders fine-tuned with hard-label, soft-label and perspectivist objectives, GPT-5.6 Terra, and four Arabic-centric large language models. Model errors are more frequent on comments with annotator disagreement. Despite relatively close Macro-F1 scores, GPT-5.6 Terra and the fine-tuned encoders exhibit contrasting error patterns: GPT-5.6 Terra, even with the annotators' definition of sexism, over-classifies gender-related content such as religious advice on modesty, whereas the encoders miss implicit and prescriptive sexism. The Arabic-centric models also over-predict sexism and remain below the encoders. Disagreement-aware learning preserves Macro-F1, but soft labels improve alignment with annotators on contested comments at the expense of unanimous ones, and neither paradigm reliably identifies contested comments. Lower performance on Egyptian Arabic, clearest for the large language models, is not fully explained by the examined measures of test-set composition and dialectness. Majority-label scores can therefore hide contrasting error patterns that matter for content moderation.

items.title: What Were You Thinking? An LLM-Driven Large-Scale Study of Refactoring Motivations in Open Source Projects
items.abstract: Context . Code refactoring improves software quality without changing external behavior. Despite its advantages, its benefits are hindered by the considerable cost of time, resources, and continuous effort it demands. Aim . Understanding why developers refactor, and which metrics capture these motivations, may support wider and more effective use of refactoring in practice. Method . We performed a large-scale empirical study to analyze developers’ refactoring activity, leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to identify underlying motivations from version control data, comparing our findings with previous motivations reported in the literature. Results . LLMs matched human judgment in 80% of cases, but aligned with literature-based motivations in only 47%. They enriched 22% of motivations with more detailed rationale, often highlighting readability, clarity, and structural improvements. Most motivations were pragmatic, focused on simplification and maintainability. While metrics related to developer experience and code readability ranked highest, their correlation with motivation categories was weak. Conclusions . We conclude that LLMs effectively capture surface-level motivations but struggle with architectural reasoning. Their value lies in providing localized explanations, which, when combined with software metrics, can form hybrid approaches. Such integration offers a promising path toward prioritizing refactoring more systematically and balancing short-term improvements with long-term architectural goals.

items.title: When "brain outsourcing" becomes habit: governmentality dilemmas and learning alienation in agentic workflows
items.abstract: The spread of generative AI has made "brain outsourcing"—delegating cognitive tasks to AI—a common phenomenon in higher education, especially in low-tier private undergraduate colleges. Existing studies explain it mainly at the individual level, neglecting the institutional consequences of the technologies used to govern it. Drawing on design-based research principles, this study conducted a three-group quasi-experiment in a Data Structures course at such a college: an adversarial workflow (Group A, n = 36), a negotiative workflow (Group B, n = 40), and a traditional control group (n = 44), triangulated across five chains of evidence. Results show that Group A's direct-dumping rate fell to 11.1% (vs. 57.5% and 75.0%), yet concealed forms—cosmetic modification and division-of-labor outsourcing—rose compensatorily, leaving the composite outsourcing index unchanged across groups (p = 0.864). Process engagement rose sharply while output authenticity stayed low (comment–code matching 3.62/5; only 27.8% of difficulty tags authentic), indicating "performative engagement". Only 1 of 120 students adopted a self-regulated strategy. In Group A, perceived control rose (+2.17) and negotiation space fell (−0.91) without meaningful growth in autonomy; the 18.3-point advantage over the control group in comprehension depth shrank to 6.8 points in transfer application. The "non-outsourceable" workflow thus changed outsourcing's form, not its deep structure, alienating learning into an adversarial game of evading detection—a new hidden curriculum. Agent design should shift from adversarial surveillance to dialogic support.

items.title: When GenAI helps and when it hurts: testing expertise reversal within a cognitive load framework across different guidance, task complexity, and GenAI access conditions
items.abstract: Abstract Studies have examined the impact of Generative AI (GenAI) on students’ learning outcomes, revealing a wide range of effects on performance, cognitive load, and learning processes. However, little is known about whether these effects change with learner expertise and the conditions under which GenAI support is provided. This study examined expertise reversal in GenAI-supported programming education across four eight-week experiments involving Year 3 computer science students from research universities in Saudi Arabia. Drawing on cognitive load theory, the experiments investigated GenAI support, guidance level, task complexity, and access condition in relation to intrinsic cognitive load, extraneous cognitive load, mental effort, and independent programming performance. The findings showed that GenAI support produced greater reductions in extraneous load and stronger independent performance among lower-expertise learners, while higher-expertise learners retained smaller benefits. Detailed guidance produced a crossover expertise reversal, benefiting lower-expertise learners while increasing extraneous load and weakening performance among higher-expertise learners. Higher task complexity increased cognitive demands and reduced performance across expertise levels, with greater effects among lower-expertise learners. Personalised access also benefited lower-expertise learners more strongly without disadvantaging higher-expertise learners. Overall, the findings distinguish a crossover expertise reversal under detailed GenAI guidance from diminishing benefits as learner expertise increases under other support and access conditions. The effects of task complexity further demonstrate that expertise-dependent differences do not necessarily constitute a reversal in instructional effectiveness. We recommend that effective GenAI support requires careful calibration to learners’ existing knowledge and the cognitive demands of learning.

items.title: When Shuffling Fails: Token Recovery from Obfuscated KV Caches
items.abstract: LLM serving systems store, offload, and share KV caches, exposing token-level representations to infrastructure operators and co-tenants. Shuffled obfuscation combines secret linear transforms with fresh permutations, claiming security from b! possible shufflings. We show that input symmetry invalidates this counting argument: security depends on distinguishable outputs under chosen inputs. Repeated tokens produce identical first-layer Value rows, making every row permutation leave the data unchanged. Only auxiliary structures such as a single-row recovery marker vary, reducing the effective state space from b! to b. We construct Repeat-to-Reveal. The attacker collects the b distinguishable states from its own probes and exploits their rank-one differences to recover an equivalent denoiser without knowing the defender's secret parameters. items.title: When Trust Does the Thinking: A Pre-Specified Test of Mindsponge Theory's Prediction That Content Counts Less as Trust Rises
items.abstract: Mindsponge theory (MT) holds that the mind evaluates incoming information most thoroughly when it neither trusts nor distrusts the source, and least at either extreme. Its testing program states this as prediction P2: the weight that content carries in acceptance follows an inverted U across trust. Rival accounts expect the weight to stay constant (Bayesian combination) or to rise with trust (monotone moderation). We report the first admitted test of P2, on the open Human-AI Interactions dataset of Vodrahalli et al. (2022). In that study, 207 US adults judged the art period of 32 paintings, received advice described as 65% or 95% accurate (identical advice in both groups), and gave a final answer. Because participants were about 66 to 70% accurate on their own, the 65% source sits near indifference and the 95% source is highly trusted, so the design covers the trusted half of the curve, where MT predicts that content weight falls. The rule, fixed and fingerprinted before any final answer was read, measured how strongly a participant’s own first judgment of the advised label governed whether the final answer sided with the advice. The weight was 4.42 logits at 65% and 3.43 at 95%; the difference was 0.99 (SE 0.34, z = 2.94, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.65), and the verdict is supported. Adding a 65/80/95 comparison gives 4.43, 3.68 and 3.45. The result survives two-way clustering and alternative codings. A post-verdict decomposition shows that trust mattered only when people’s own judgment opposed the advice; within those trials the drop in weight is clearer on a continuous measure (z = 2.17) than on the pre-specified binary one (z = 0.64). Because trials in which participants already agreed with the advice cannot show acceptance, these disagreement trials are the cleaner test of P2. The result clearly disfavors monotone moderation, disfavors constant Bayesian weighting with moderate rather than strong evidence, and does not separate MT from simple opinion averaging. It supports the trusted half of P2, not the full inverted U.

items.title: Where Does Epistemic Capacity Reside? Functional Externalization in Generative AI Systems
items.abstract: Generative AI systems are increasingly used to retrieve, synthesize, evaluate, and communicate information in knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet observed epistemic performance is often attributed either to the human user or to the AI model, even when it depends on a wider configuration of models, retrieval mechanisms, external sources, tools, interfaces, permissions, and human oversight. This paper asks under what conditions epistemic capacity should be attributed to a configured system rather than to either the human or the model alone, and what follows from locating that capacity. Drawing on distributed cognition, extended and social epistemology, and work on epistemic technologies, the paper develops a task-relative attribution framework grounded in functional externalization. For a specified task class, operating conditions, and acceptable performance criterion, it identifies a minimal adequate capacity-bearing configuration as an organized set of functionally integrated components sufficient to realize the relevant capacity, such that no proper subconfiguration remains sufficient under the same specification. Minimality does not imply uniqueness: different configurations may be equally minimal and adequate. Through comparative functional reconstruction of context-bounded synthesis, retrieval-augmented generation, and tool-augmented systems, the paper distinguishes operational components from epistemic resources and background conditions and shows why individual component necessity is not required when redundant routes realize the same functional role. The paper advances two claims. First, epistemic capacity should be attributed at the minimal organized level required to explain its realization across the relevant class of tasks, rather than inferred from the most visible component. Second, locating that capacity does not determine the loci of understanding, epistemic authority, purpose, control, authorship, or responsibility. These properties may coincide with, overlap, or diverge from the capacity-bearing configuration, but only for independent reasons. The contribution is therefore not to rediscover distributed cognition or sociotechnical epistemic practice, but to provide a deliberately minimal framework for disciplined attribution without presupposing a theory of extended mind, artificial understanding, or epistemic subjecthood.

items.title: Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game, so we propose a harder challenge, the Personal Imitation Game, which asks whether a machine can replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human. Testing with 30 participants, we establish a human baseline and report the identity signals interrogators rely on: stylometric features, personality traits, and biographical facts. To demonstrate the framework, we design an LLM-based system that plays the game for one of the paper's authors, drawing on an autoethnographic dataset spanning ten years of personal digital communication. In a 20-person deception study, interrogators choose our system over the author's own friends in 7 of 10 rounds, and the author over our system in 13 of 20; neither rate is distinguishable from chance at this sample size. We consider design improvements, applications of personal AI agents, and implications for identity and privacy.

items.title: Who chose the label? Voluntary versus mandated AI disclosure in tourism marketing
items.abstract: Generative AI is being used extensively by destination marketing organisations (DMOs) to create promotional imagery, and new regulation requires disclosure of some synthetic content. Previous research indicates that revealing an AI source can reduce perceived authenticity but treats disclosure as a single cue. This study investigated whether travellers react differently when the AI label is presented as the DMO's own decision or as a legally mandated requirement. A simulated single factor, three condition (no label, voluntary label, mandated label) between-subjects online experiment with N = 387 adult participants. The analysis was based on the Persuasion Knowledge Model and attribution theory, using ANCOVA, bootstrapped parallel mediation analyses (multicategorical predictor), moderation by attitudes towards AI and robustness checks. Both labels reduced perceived authenticity compared to no label (voluntary: d = −0.59; mandated: d = −0.74). The voluntary label raised perceived DMO integrity (d = 0.38), producing a positive indirect effect on visit intention. The mandated label earned no integrity credit, and its negative indirect effect through authenticity was not compensated. These effects were not significantly moderated by general attitudes toward AI. The study distinguishes between what the AI label says and who is seen to have chosen it, thereby furthering the research on persuasion-knowledge in tourism and providing a model that DMOs can test for disclosure in the regulatory era.
