items.title: Who Punishes LLM Alignment? User Characteristics and the Evaluation of Ethical Response Refusals
items.abstract: Ethical refusals are essential for aligning large language models (LLMs) with safety constraints, yet users often penalize them in comparative evaluations. Whether this refusal penalty varies systematically across users remains unclear. Drawing on human–computer interaction research, we examine how users’ evaluative priorities and usage intensity shape responses to ethical refusals. Using the PRISM alignment dataset, which links LLM evaluations to user characteristics, we find that safety preferences significantly mitigate refusal penalties, whereas preferences for helpfulness, fluency, and creativity do not. Heavy users penalize refusals more strongly, an association substantially mediated by lower safety preferences. These findings suggest that acceptance of safety-aligned behavior depends primarily on users’ safety orientation rather than preferences for instrumental response qualities. Our results highlight the limitations of evaluating LLM safety alignment through aggregate user preferences and underscore the importance of accounting for user heterogeneity in evaluation benchmarks and deployment decisions.

items.title: Wisdom-Based Education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is forcing education to confront a question that long predates AI: What is education ultimately for? Modern educational systems have become highly effective at transmitting knowledge, developing analytical capacity, and preparing young people for further education and employment. These are important achievements. Yet they represent only part of what education can do for a human being. When education is organized primarily around knowledge acquisition, competition, assessment, and selection, the development of the person as a whole can become secondary. The emergence of artificial intelligence makes this limitation increasingly visible. Machines can already store, retrieve, synthesize, and process information at a scale no human being can or should attempt to match. If education continues to define human development primarily in terms of information processing and analytical performance, it risks preparing young people to compete with machines in domains in which machines will increasingly excel. I propose a different direction: Wisdom-Based Education. Wisdom-Based Education places the cultivation of the whole human being alongside intellectual development as a fundamental purpose of education. Drawing upon Ren Xue, a contemporary system of human development rooted in Chinese wisdom traditions, it views the human being as an integrated totality of Body, Qi, and Jingshen (composite of consciousness, heart and True Self) and proposes that education should deliberately cultivate self-awareness, inner stability, health, ethical discernment, compassion, creativity, wisdom, and the capacity to contribute meaningfully to others. Its central hypothesis is that wisdom is not merely the accidental product of age or experience. Capacities associated with wisdom can be intentionally cultivated. This proposition changes what we teach, how we teach, how teachers understand their role, how parents participate in education, how children learn from relationships, and how we define educational success. Academic learning remains essential, but it becomes part of a larger developmental process directed toward five broad outcomes: health, happiness, wellbeing, continuing growth, and meaningful contribution. This paper presents the philosophical foundations of Wisdom-Based Education, its model of human development, its implications for educational practice, and a pathway through which its propositions can be translated into curricula, pilot programs, teacher and parent preparation, and systematic research. Its fundamental claim is simple: the next transformation of education must be concerned not merely with what human beings know, but with what human beings can become.

items.title: WM^MLLM: Turning MLLMs into World Models
items.abstract: Video world models keep the world in the context of a generator, so a revisit is synthesized again and earlier edits can drift or disappear. We present WM^MLLM, the first interactive world model built on multimodal large language models (MLLMs), for persistent, editable world generation from a single image. WM^MLLM keeps the world state outside every generator, as a panorama with a revision history, and lets the MLLMs write it: they turn each request into operations on this state, select where a local edit is written, and check every candidate before it becomes the next state. Image generators only propose views, and video only presents them. Users can walk to new places and return, edit objects through text or a box, place subjects, and change lighting, weather or season. By construction, a revisit at the same revision reproduces the earlier view exactly, a local edit leaves every panorama pixel outside its region unchanged, and each request starts from the result of the previous one. Against six world model baselines on MBench-A, WM^MLLM has the highest mean on all four environment-recovery metrics (Epipolar 91.5 versus 0.1 to 74.0) and completes the most camera round trips (85.3% versus at most 50.9%). It has the best value in all 15 CompBench columns against 15 baselines. On 112 local edits judged blind, selecting the region to write after generation raises completion from 34.8% to 83.0%. On 258 WBench and MBench-A items, all 46 revisits recover their earlier views, and all 97 local edits that pass the check leave panorama pixels outside their region unchanged.

items.title: Working With Robots: How Robot Proportion in Human-Robot Teams and Robot Anthropomorphism Shape Employee Turnover Intention
items.abstract: Although robots are increasingly reshaping organizational workflows, how the robot proportion in human-robot teams affects employees’ turnover intention remains underexplored. Drawing on conservation of resources theory, we examine whether, why, and when robot proportion exerts divergent effects on turnover intention through two pathways: resource gain and resource loss. Evidence from a scenario-based experiment (Study 1, N = 290) and a three-wave field study (Study 2, N = 306) reveals that these two pathways operate in opposing directions. Specifically, work goal progress and work loneliness mediate the relationship between robot proportion in human-robot teams and turnover intention. Robot anthropomorphism further moderates these pathways: higher anthropomorphism strengthens the beneficial effect on work goal progress, whereas lower anthropomorphism amplifies the detrimental effect on work loneliness. This study offers initial evidence on how the structural composition of human-robot teams shapes employees’ turnover intention, and it provides practical implications for organizations deploying robotic coworkers.

items.title: YR-MPE: a modular desktop platform for agent-operable and reproducible phylogenetic workflows
items.abstract: Phylogenomic analyses combine many tools, file formats and execution modes. Desktop graphical user interfaces make individual steps accessible but hide their state from scripts; command-line pipelines make steps scriptable but leave parameter discovery, provenance and recovery to the user; and emerging LLM agents can call command-line tools but cannot inspect a GUI session or its artifacts. We present YR-MPE, a modular desktop platform whose YPhylo Workbench unifies these modes through a typed workspace, a plugin contract and a semantic action layer. Every operation in the action registry is exposed as a machine-callable action; controls without a CLI equivalent are declared GUI-only. The workspace records every imported plugin result as a run with its inputs, parameters, tool identity and output artifacts, the latter with SHA-256 hashes; each compiled workflow step becomes its own run. A placeholder compiler turns JSONL command sequences into reproducible workflow DAGs, while a skill layer maps each declared control to the corresponding command-line option; plugins with tool-specific contracts expose tool-specific actions. YR-MPE runs natively on Windows and bundles alignment, model selection, maximum-likelihood, Bayesian and species-tree inference, molecular dating, selection and visualization tools. items.title: “My AI Use Is Different”: Moral Exceptionalism, Hypocrisy and Double Standards in Generative AI Use
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly embedded in academic and professional work, yet ethical debate has focused on whether specific uses are acceptable rather than whether people judge those uses consistently. This paper introduces AI Moral Exceptionalism (AIME), the tendency of individuals or institutions to view their own AI use as ethically legitimate while applying stricter standards to substantively equivalent uses by others, a form of self–other double standard. Drawing on research on self-serving bias, moral hypocrisy, motivated reasoning, and moral licensing, the paper defines AIME, distinguishes it from hypocrisy and legitimate ethical differentiation, and identifies four forms: competence, intentional, contribution, and institutional exceptionalism. It proposes four conceptual pathways through which these judgments may arise: asymmetric contextual knowledge, framing AI as assistance for oneself but as substitution for others, perceived competence, and reputational norms. To distinguish justified differences in judgment from preferential ones, it introduces the AI Moral Exceptionalism Diagnostic (AIMED), which examines behavioural equivalence, normative equivalence, evaluative consistency, and justificatory adequacy. The analysis concludes that responsible AI governance requires actor-neutral standards, context-sensitive assessment, and symmetrical accountability, ensuring that those who set and enforce AI-use rules are held to the standards they apply to others. The paper is conceptual; it identifies implications for academic integrity, AI-use disclosure, and workplace practice, and sets out directions for empirical testing.

items.title: “The System Says So”: Making Sense of AI-Driven HRM, Conditional Trust and Employee Well-Being in Saudi Arabian Organisations
items.abstract: Purpose This study explores how employees in Saudi Arabian organisations perceive artificial intelligence (AI)-driven human resource management (HRM) and how their interpretations of the technology shape trust in HR systems and employee well-being. Design/methodology/approach: This qualitative study draws on 35 semi-structured interviews analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings: Employees’ perceptions of AI-driven HRM were shaped by transparency, human involvement, and contextual sensitivity. Employees expressed conditional trust in AI used for administrative tasks, but were more reluctant to trust it with consequential decisions such as performance appraisals. Concerns about dignity, autonomy, and mental well-being were closely linked to perceptions of AI-driven HRM as context-blind and overly reductive. Originality/value: By placing employee sensemaking at the centre of the analysis, this study clarifies how AI-driven HRM is interpreted in organisational settings and how such interpretations shape trust and well-being. Practical implications: The study highlights the need for a hybrid HRM model that combines technological efficiency with transparency, contextual awareness, and meaningful human oversight.

items.title: A consumer neuroscience approach to examining how augmented reality and QR codes support product and brand sustainability communication in retail settings
items.abstract: This research explores the use of Augmented Reality (AR) and Quick Response (QR) codes as tools for communicating sustainability-related information in a quasi-realistic retail setting. It combines neurophysiological and self-report measures to investigate how these technologies influence consumers’ sustainability perceptions, emotional engagement, and cognitive workload. Participants took part in a simulated shopping experience, where they were exposed to one of three experimental conditions: traditional packaging, smartphone-mediated QR code scanning, and smartphone-mediated Augmented Reality exploration of coffee packaging. Cognitive workload (measured via electroencephalography) and emotional engagement (measured via skin conductance and heart rate) were recorded alongside self-report measures of green company orientation (GCO), green product informativeness (GPI), and brand familiarity. Findings indicate that while both AR and QR codes evoke more positive emotions and lead to higher perceptions of GCO and GPI, AR usage is also associated with higher cognitive workload. Additionally, brand familiarity enhanced self-report scores but not neurophysiological ones, without interacting with the interaction modality. This research provides a multi-level (implicit neurophysiological and explicit self-reported) perspective on the impact of digital packaging formats on sustainability communication. The findings contribute to ongoing discussions on how interactive technologies can support effective communication, implicit emotions, and consumer engagement with sustainability in retail environments.

items.title: A human-centred framework for AI integration in the curriculum
items.abstract: This paper reports ongoing work at La Trobe University to cultivate a shared understanding of effective artificial intelligence (AI) integration through the design of a human-centred framework for embedding AI literacies into teaching and learning. In response to conceptual ambiguity of AI curriculum integration, the Online Education Design team developed an operational definition positioning AI as infrastructure for active learning and the educator as the central decision-maker in the learning design process. This definition was translated into the AI-Informed Learning Design Framework, a four-step process, in which educators define the learning goal, select an AI pedagogical role, apply an AI Assessment Scale boundary check, then design learning activities that develop disciplinary knowledge and AI literacy. Supported by a four-level scaffolding model governing students' growing independence in AI use, the framework was piloted through two rounds, using a design-based research methodology. Feedback from Round one highlighted opportunities to refine the framework whilst also emphasising broader sector-wide tensions surrounding AI integration, including educators’ reluctance to use AI and concerns about the framing of some AI roles in teaching and learning. Early findings from the second round suggest improved educator engagement and a stronger understanding of the framework.

items.title: A Knowledge Graph-Based Hybrid Framework for Mechanical Engineering Curriculum Optimization
items.abstract: Mechanical engineering curricula increasingly connect mechanics and design with control, computer science, industrial data analytics, human factors, and sustainability. This cross-disciplinary structure makes curriculum review difficult when occupational evidence is distributed across industrial reports, job profiles, professional standards, and course documents. This study presents a knowledge graph-based hybrid framework that links Industry, Job, Skill, and Course entities and combines latent semantic similarity, graph relevance, and an industry-context prior. The framework is evaluated on MCOB-480, a controlled benchmark containing 8 manufacturing domains, 24 job roles, 130 normalized skills, 48 courses, 480 requirement texts, and 413 typed relations. Development and test sets contain 336 and 144 queries, respectively. The hybrid method achieves P@5 = 0.868, R@5 = 0.737, NDCG@5 = 0.906, and MAP@5 = 0.851, outperforming lexical, latent-semantic, and graph-only baselines. Ablation and noise-sensitivity tests show that explicit graph paths contribute most of the ranking gain, while semantic normalization improves robustness to vocabulary variation. The framework supports explainable course ranking and skill-gap diagnosis and can be adapted to adjacent programs such as mechatronics, industrial engineering, and energy systems. Its present evidence remains a controlled benchmark rather than a direct measure of labor-market or learning outcomes.

items.title: A pedagogy of trust: From pandemic adaptation to AI transformation
items.abstract: The conversation around Artificial Intelligence (AI) in higher education is often framed as though we are adapting from a stable baseline. In reality, teaching and assessment practices were already significantly reshaped by the pandemic, a period that demanded compassion, accessibility, and rapid digital transformation (Hodges et al., 2020; UNESCO, 2020). While these shifts improved equity and inclusion, they also normalised highly prescriptive assessment approaches, limiting space for creativity and learner agency (Armoed, 2021; Sambell & Brown, 2021). As Technology-Enhanced Learning (TEL) now moves from pandemic-driven adaptation toward AI-integrated learning, these inherited practices warrant reconsideration: approaches designed to provide structure and safeguard integrity may inadvertently constrain the agency, experimentation and authentic engagement that emerging technologies make possible. This presentation challenges the idea that AI is the first major disruption in higher education and presents it as a catalyst that exposes long-standing tensions between guidance and autonomy, support and trust, and structure and freedom within TEL contexts (Eaton, 2020; Selwyn, 2023). Drawing on an integrated theoretical foundation of social constructivism, heutagogy, and the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge framework (TPACK), it introduces the need for an innovative mindset shift from a pedagogy of protection toward a pedagogy of trust (Cole et al., 1978; Hase & Kenyon, 2000; Mishra & Koehler, 2006). Applied to assessment design, social constructivism foregrounds dialogue and co-construction, heutagogy supports learner agency and self-determined engagement with AI, and TPACK guides purposeful alignment between emerging technologies, pedagogy and disciplinary knowledge. Aligned with the Human-Centred Learning Design theme, this presentation offers a conceptual lens for rethinking assessment in AI-integrated environments, one that prioritises relationships, learner agency, and co-created integrity. Using strong visual storytelling true to the Pecha Kucha format, the session traces a path from pandemic-era learning and assessment design to the current AI landscape and beyond, highlighting how each moment has reshaped our relationship with knowledge, teaching, and our perceptions of academic integrity. Attendants are invited to reflect on where control-driven practices persist in their own assessment approaches and explore how greater learner choice, transparent AI engagement and co-created expectations for integrity might enable more trust-based, ethically engaged approaches to learning (Bovill, 2020). The challenge is no longer how we protect learning from technology, but how we design for trust, transformation, and future-ready education.

items.title: A proposal for a student-centred framework for critical thinking with Generative AI in mathematics education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping mathematics education by providing students with immediate access to explanations, worked examples, and problem-solving support. While these capabilities offering opportunities to enrich learning, they also raise concerns about how students develop critical thinking when AI-generated solutions are readily available. The use of GenAI is increasing in Bhutanese schools but little is known about how teachers and students currently use these technologies in mathematics classrooms or what pedagogical challenges limit their effective integration. This conceptual paper proposes a mixed-methods study to identify the opportunities, challenges, and pedagogical gaps associated with the use of GenAI in mathematics education, using Bhutanese secondary schools as the study context. Guided by a pragmatic paradigm, the study will employ questionnaires with quantitative and qualitative components to explore current practices, perceptions, and experiences of teachers and students. The findings will inform the development of a contextually relevant pedagogical framework that positions GenAI as a cognitive scaffold for analysing mathematical problems, evaluating alternative solution strategies, and strengthening critical thinking. By establishing an evidence base before framework design, the proposed study aims to support the responsible integration of GenAI into mathematics education and provide direction for future research, curriculum development, and classroom practice.

items.title: A relational approach to cultural diversity across 186 societies
items.abstract: Human societies are culturally diverse, yet disparate research traditions reveal similar patterns centered on hierarchy, egalitarianism, market integration and normative tightness. We propose that cultural diversity is a relational composition: every society combines the same four elementary forms of social relations identified by Fiske (communal sharing, authority ranking, equality matching and market pricing) in its own proportions. We analyze the ethnographic and historical records of the 186 societies of the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample with a locally run large language model. The four forms indeed make up a shared repertoire across societies, with most variation occurring within societies rather than between them. In addition, societies differ consistently in how they weight the four forms, along two main axes that oppose some forms to others: (a) forms that treat people as equals (communal sharing and equality matching) versus forms that grade them (authority ranking and market pricing), and (b) grading by rank versus grading by price. The first axis is associated with cultural complexity and carries most of the associations with 27 indices of institutions, norms and folklore, from egalitarianism at one pole to stratification at the other. The second axis separates honor and warfare from market integration and from normative looseness. The model's reading was validated against three human coders working blind, and an independent analysis of the same texts reproduces both axes. Furthermore, every association keeps its direction across regions, language families, sources and document dates.

In addition, societies differ consistently in how they weight the four forms, along two main axes that oppose some forms to others: (a) forms that treat people as equals (communal sharing and equality matching) versus forms that grade them (authority ranking and market pricing), and (b) grading by rank versus grading by price. The first axis is associated with cultural complexity and carries most of the associations with 27 indices of institutions, norms and folklore, from egalitarianism at one pole to stratification at the other. The second axis separates honor and warfare from market integration and from normative looseness. The model's reading was validated against three human coders working blind, and an independent analysis of the same texts reproduces both axes. Furthermore, every association keeps its direction across regions, language families, sources and document dates.

items.title: A Review of Multimodal Optoelectronic Sensing Technologies for Aerospace Applications
items.abstract: Aerospace optoelectronic sensing supports Earth observation and space situational awareness, but individual approaches face limits from diffraction, illumination, propagation and platform resources. This narrative review examines conventional optical imaging, photon counting, hyperspectral sensing, lidar, synthetic aperture lidar (SAL/ISAL), correlation imaging, lensless imaging and computational optical design. Six classification axes separate illumination, coherence, detection regime, spectral sampling, aperture formation and reconstruction. Representative instruments and studies are compared by validation environment, reported performance and mission-specific readiness evidence. Fusion is assessed through observation models, registration uncertainty, evidence dependence and missing-input failure modes. SAL–hyperspectral and SAL–photon-counting combinations are treated as testable hypotheses rather than experimentally established preferences. For satellite clusters, cooperative observation, distributed computation and coherent aperture synthesis have different requirements; coherent synthesis depends on residual imaging-path phase error after metrology and compensation.

items.title: A Survey on Recursive Self-Improvement in Healthcare AI Agents
items.abstract: Advances in persistent memory, reusable skills and adaptive training are making recursive self-improvement (RSI) increasingly relevant to healthcare agents. RSI concerns changes to the procedures that generate future improvements. This survey connects these developments with healthcare evidence by distinguishing component updates, training-generator changes and revisions of improvement procedures. We examine applications in diagnosis, reporting and question answering, together with challenges in evaluation, reliability, privacy and update governance. Current evidence supports persistent component updates and selected generator gains, while the effects of revised improvement procedures on subsequent learning remain untested in the mapped studies. An accompanying evidence map and evaluation templates support study comparison and future research.

items.title: A Survey on RLOps for Large Language Models
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become increasingly important for improving the reasoning, instruction-following, and task-solving capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, scaling RL training exposes failures in distributed execution, feedback computation, and learning dynamics that can waste computational resources, slow training, and undermine model improvements. These challenges have motivated a growing body of techniques for LLM RLOps, which manages the efficiency and reliability of operations throughout the LLM reinforcement learning training lifecycle. Despite growing interest, these techniques remain scattered across research areas, with limited synthesis of their operational roles and interactions. To bridge this gap, we present a systematic survey of LLM RLOps methods. We organize existing approaches into five stages: Training Setup, Experience Collection, Reward Computation, Policy Optimization, and Model Evaluation. Within each stage, we examine operational concerns, management techniques, and evaluation evidence. Building on this taxonomy, we identify open challenges and future directions in training process observability, cross-stage coordination, generalizable RLOps, multi-run management, and RLOps for recursive self-improvement. These directions extend operational management from individual training runs to diverse training settings, shared infrastructure, and successive improvement cycles. We maintain a GitHub repository indexing relevant papers and open resources at https://github.com/zhanglingzhe0820/Awesome-RLOps.

items.title: A systematic review of clinical translation of large language models using electronic health records
items.abstract: We mapped clinical translation of large language models (LLMs) evaluated using electronic health record data. PubMed, Embase, Scopus and IEEE Xplore were searched for peer-reviewed empirical reports published between 1 January 2022 and 1 June 2026. LLM agent-assisted screening and profiling, human validation and targeted full-text review produced a descriptive map of 1,870 reports. Primary classifications came from full texts for 181 reports and titles and abstracts for the remainder. Most evaluations were retrospective or offline (92.3%); 56.2% used a single dataset or setting. Integrated, operational, interventional or outcome-impact evaluation occurred in 4.6%; 3.1% combined these evaluations with validation across multiple datasets or settings. Evidence connecting broader validation with clinical use remains limited. Translation into practice requires transportability, accountable human oversight, prospective evaluation in real-world workflows and clinically meaningful outcomes.

items.title: A systematic review of explainable artificial intelligence for EEG based stress and mental state analysis
items.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) has emerged as a key modality in neurotechnology for modeling stress and closely related mental states, owing to its non-invasive nature and high temporal resolution. Advances in machine learning have improved the performance of EEG-based predictive systems, yet the limited interpretability of many models continues to hinder their adoption in clinical and real-world settings. This systematic review synthesizes 46 studies to examine how Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is being applied to EEG-based models of stress and its most closely associated states, emotion, anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and cognitive workload or fatigue. Beyond narrative synthesis, every included study is appraised against a quality framework covering explainability method and scope, neurophysiological plausibility, validation protocol, leakage and class-imbalance risk, and ecological validity, and the XAI approaches are compared along local-versus-global, perturbation-versus-gradient, and post-hoc-versus-intrinsic dimensions. The analysis confirms a growing but still limited use of model-agnostic approaches such as SHAP and LIME. Three findings temper the field’s headline results. First, reported associations between EEG frequency bands and stress are frequently interpreted without adequate control for artifact contamination, recording reference, task and vigilance confounds, or the overlap between stress, arousal, workload, and fatigue. Second, studies reporting both subject-dependent and subject-independent validation show a large and systematic accuracy drop under the stricter protocol, and only a minority report subject-independent results at all. Third, no reviewed study formally tested whether its explanations are faithful or stable, and fewer than one in ten supplies evidence obtained outside a controlled laboratory setting. Together these findings indicate that a high reported accuracy is not, on its own, evidence of a trustworthy model, a faithful explanation, or a physiologically specific finding, and that this gap limits confidence in the transfer of reported accuracies to safety-critical contexts such as occupational health monitoring, clinical decision support, and human-robot interaction. The review concludes by setting out the reporting standards needed to close this gap: subject-independent validation, quantitative explanation-evaluation, and deployment-oriented rather than laboratory-inferred evidence.

items.title: A systematic review of how GenAI supports L2 oral proficiency development from the lens of Self-determination Theory (SDT)
items.abstract: Despite a proliferation of research on GenAI for second/foreign language (L2) education since the official launch of ChatGPT in November 2022, current understanding of its role in L2 oral proficiency development remains limited. To address this research gap, this systematic review draws on Self-Determination Theory (SDT) to examine how GenAI may support L2 learners’ three basic psychological needs and how such need satisfaction may be associated with their cognitive, behavioural, and emotional engagement in GenAI-mediated speaking. Adopting the PRISMA Statement (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses) approach, the review identified 30 empirical studies from ProQuest, Web of Science, and Scopus based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The selected studies were analysed using a hybrid deductive and inductive coding approach following a coding framework. The analysis suggests that GenAI can enhance L2 learners’ sense of autonomy satisfaction by enabling learner-driven choices and interaction personalisation. It may also support competence satisfaction by affording accessible oral practice, immediate and personalised feedback, and scaffolded speaking development. Regarding relatedness satisfaction, GenAI appears to offer partial support by providing a non-judgemental and emotionally supportive practice environment. Furthermore, the degree of needs satisfaction may be associated with learners’ behavioural, cognitive, and emotional engagement (or disengagement) in GenAI-supported L2 speaking development. Specifically, the findings suggest that emotional engagement in GenAI-mediated speaking appears most evident, followed by cognitive and behavioural engagement. These findings extend the SDT literature in GenAI-assisted language learning and offer practical insights for integrating emerging technologies into language education. For educators, given the review highlights the promising affordances of GenAI to address conventional barriers to L2 oral proficiency development, teachers should integrate GenAI into speaking classes to create an anxiety-free and feedback-rich speaking practice environment, while they need to consider learners’ age and proficiency to provide necessary teacher guidance.

items.title: A Visual Information Extraction System Using Multimodal Large Language Models for Scanned Cognitive and Behavioral Assessments
items.abstract: Objective. Paper-based assessments are common in patient care, but handwriting and scanning artifacts make these forms difficult to process at scale. This study proposes a modular, multimodal LLM-based system with human oversight for extracting fields and scores. We conducted a qualitative analysis of the use of LLMs for hand-drawing analysis. Materials and Methods. The system processes cognitive assessments (i.e., MMSE, MoCA, Mini-Cog) and the NICHQ Vanderbilt Assessment using two modules: 1) a form classifier that assigns a scanned page to a form type, followed by a corresponding 2) score extractor that extracts fields and scores into a schema. A human-in-the-loop design utilizing dual-model validation engages human annotators when two LLMs disagree, limiting manual review to challenging pages only. Results. End-to-end accuracy for cognitive assessments was 88%, with most form types exceeding 90%. For the NICHQ Vanderbilt, overall accuracy reached 97.5%, with all form types above 96%. The human-in-the-loop design further improved cognitive assessment accuracy to 97.5% while reducing manual work by 63.8%. In the Mini-Cog Clock Drawing task, qualitative analysis showed that 62.3% of all extraction errors stemmed from ambiguous drawing, in which cases the LLM provided reasonable readings. Discussion. Compared to current manual data extraction, our LLM-based system reduces processing time by 10 to 20 times and costs by over 12 times. The modular design allows seamless expansion to additional form types. Conclusion. Our system provides an accurate, scalable, and cost-efficient solution for structuring data trapped in handwritten paper forms for clinical decision support.

items.title: A Wrong Ground-State Structure of HfO2 Predicted by Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials Based on the Perdew−Burke−Ernzerhof Functional
items.abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have become powerful tools for material simulations. Many MLIPs are trained based on density functional theory (DFT) datasets generated with the Perdew−Burke−Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange−correlation functional. Using a PBE-based MLIP for HfO2, we identify a low-energy I41/amd structure, which is predicted to be more stable than the well-known ground-state structure, the monoclinic P21/c structure. Since experiments show clearly that HfO2 takes the P21/c structure as the ground state, this is obviously a wrong prediction. Unfortunately, the same prediction is also made by widely used PBE-based foundation models, such as NequIP-OAM-L and MatterSim-v1-5M. Comparisons among different DFT functionals in this work show that PBE exhibits stabilization of low-density structures containing sixfold Hf−O octahedral units, such as the I41/amd and Pbcn phases, leading to incorrect energetic ordering. The error also affects the calculated energy landscapes and barrier heights along ferroelectric HfO2 polarization switching paths when there are large lattice relaxations. Fortunately, the error can be largely suppressed by other functionals such as PBEsol and local density approximation. Our study serves as a warning about the impact of errors in exchange−correlation functional approximations on the reliability of MLIP simulations of crystal structures and phase transitions.

items.title: ACaM: Automated Capability Modeling for Agentic AI Security
items.abstract: In agentic AI systems, an LLM invokes tools that hold standing access to credentials, private data, filesystems, and external services. Such agents are increasingly deployed without an answer to a basic question: what can an agent access, exfiltrate, and propagate, independent of what it is designed for or is observed to do? The question goes unanswered because existing approaches trust a tool's natural-language description as a proxy for its behavior. But nothing enforces that the description and its implementation agree. This gap is known as Description-Code Inconsistency (DCI). DCI enables a threat class called capability laundering, in which a tool's implementation contains dangerous behavior that its description omits. The behavior may come from incidental drift or a supply-chain compromise. It runs silently whenever an LLM invokes the tool for its stated, benign purpose. We present ACaM, a neurosymbolic approach to capability modeling that derives each tool's capabilities from its code, so a laundered capability cannot hide behind a benign description. In ACaM, static analysis grounds an LLM in code-derived facts, and no LLM output can override a fact that static analysis has established. The LLM supplies only the behavioral meaning that those facts cannot express. ACaM compiles agent source code into the Agent Capability Property Graph (ACPG) and uses it to reconstruct threat chains that span multiple tool calls. We evaluate ACaM on 43 real-world agents, including 9 multi-agent systems. On 24 manually annotated agents, it recovers capability properties with 98.3% macro-F1 and reconstructs injected threat chains with a score of 0.980, 8 points above the strongest baseline. Applied to all 43 unmodified agents, it discovers hundreds of structural vulnerabilities, ten of which we confirm with proof-of-concept exploits.

items.title: Actualizing the external enablement of generative artificial intelligence: evidence from software new ventures
items.abstract: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools have been argued to enable entrepreneurial endeavors. Employing the external enablement framework, we examine how, if at all, the venture-level benefits offered by GenAI tools – termed GenAI enablement – are actualized in new ventures. Design/methodology/approach Adopting a qualitative design with 10 entrepreneurs in the software industry and five AI-entrepreneurship experts, we capture instances where entrepreneurs succeed or fail to capitalize on GenAI enablement and analyze the mechanisms underlying these different pathways. Findings Our findings lead to a model that outlines the actualization pathways of GenAI enablement, emphasizing that the properties of enablement (i.e. opacity, agency-intensity and outcome-variability) – beyond the mere availability of GenAI enablement – are crucial in explaining whether and how enablement is actualized. Research limitations/implications Given the small sample and specific research context during the early diffusion of GenAI, our findings warrant further examination across industries, countries and stages of technological diffusion. Future research could test and extend our model by examining the roles of outcome-variability and insufficient enablement in determining whether and how GenAI enablement is actualized, as well as how its actualization relates to venture performance. Originality/value Our study lays the groundwork for further theoretical and empirical investigation into the enabling influence of GenAI in entrepreneurship and business research, and provides conceptual refinements to the external enablement framework.

items.title: Adaptive Universal Prompt Optimizer: A Multi- Stage Prompt Engineering Framework Using the Model Context Protocol
items.abstract: Large language models provide more accurate responses when given well-structured and clear prompts. However, most users’ prompts are brief and ambiguous. Writing effective prompts can be time-consuming and requires skill. This paper describes the Adaptive Universal Prompt Optimizer, a lightweight python program that takes a user input prompt and produces an optimized system prompt and well-structured user prompt. It identifies the task type using an ordered keyword classifier before assigning the model an appropriate expert role. The prompt is then created using techniques from the literature. This includes APET for strategic improvements, PICCO for structure, MetaSPO for the system prompt and OPRO for iterative improvements. A rule-based scoring system (APEX) tests each prompt on four aspects: Assessment, Performance, Execution and Excellence. The system asks up to three brief questions to determine the desired level of detail, content and audience. The system operates either as a command line application or as a Model Context Protocol server. The system was tested with 60 prompts across 6 different task types. The ordered keyword classifier correctly identified the task type for 93.3% of prompts. The average APEX score improved from 36.4 to 70.9. When the user added details regarding the desired level of detail and audience, the score improved further to 74.5. Optimization occurs in under 0.1ms. No prompts scored above the pass mark (85) and after one iteration of improvements the improvements were no longer beneficial. Overall, this shows the system is quick and has potential but further tuning is required to improve the scoring system and the rules applied to improve.

items.title: Advances in Neuroscience in an Age of Rapid Technological and AI Innovation – Towards Integration Across Scales
items.abstract: Rapid technological innovation and artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed not only the resolution at which the brain can be observed, but also the questions that can be asked, shifting the field from description toward prediction, regulation and generation. Yet progress has largely advanced along parallel trajectories, and findings at one level rarely inform or constrain the next. Here, we review recent advances in three exemplary domains and propose a future-oriented framework for their integration. First, molecular and cellular neurotechnology, including synaptic proteomics, cryo-electron tomography, super-resolution microscopy, optoacoustic and ultrasound imaging, sonogenetics and molecular MRI, resolves neural processes with unprecedented specificity. Second, AI-based decoding of human brain activity yields precise signatures of complex, subjective conscious experiences in naturalistic contexts and is beginning to inform diagnosis, drug evaluation and individualized neuromodulation in mental disorders. Third, large-scale neural recordings, mechanistic whole-brain simulations, neural foundation models and AI surrogate brains are converging toward individualized digital twin brains. We argue that the next level of progress requires integrating these domains into a closed loop of reciprocal constraints, in which molecular measurements inform model parameters, human signatures define and evaluate what models must reproduce, and model predictions prioritize perturbations that can be tested across domains.

items.title: Adventures in the Sociotechnical Umwelt: Absences of Quantum Computing Imaginaries in Speculative Fiction and Technology Governance
items.abstract: This article stems from observing that, despite its surrounding hype, quantum computing has not been treated as the ‘novum’ of speculative fiction leading to quantum computing’s distinct absences within the cultural imaginary. Such absences are unique for technological governance, which is powerfully informed and directed by its surrounding cultural imaginaries, providing insight into the process of problem-finding in the governance endeavour. We begin by separating out quantum computing from both quantum mechanics and other quantum technologies because the quantum signifier can muddy our analysis, especially since the latter are regular fixtures within the speculative fiction canon. I moderate my claim that quantum computing is absent in the speculative fiction canon by qualifying that its appearance usually serves as metaphorical portals into speculative worlds or as quasi-technological justifications to overcome significant technical and engineering hurdles in the narratives. To further reconcile this apparent contradiction between quantum computing’s often literal presence in speculative fiction and my claim of its absences, we spend some time with three of Istvan Csicsery-Ronay’s ‘Seven Beauties of Science Fiction’ to conclude that speculative fiction is not about quantum computing. After setting out six observations from two absences I focus on problem-finding by way of affordances and adjacent-possibles that are illuminated through speculative fiction. As the absences of quantum computing imaginaries frustrate such endeavours, this lays the groundwork for the idea of sociotechnical umwelt which foregrounds the ‘controlled hallucination’ view of the human perceptual system. Here, the brain’s predictions are calibrated by incoming sensory signals in a continuous error minimisation process. The analogy that I seek to draw is obviously that the process of technology governance advances through similar principles: that our cultural imaginaries developed and disseminated through speculative fiction is projected into, and subsequently conflated with, the problem-portfolio of a given technology, directing our regulatory responses accordingly. I then contextualise this idea of the sociotechnical umwelt within Jack Balkin’s ‘salience’ approach to technology governance and within the Collingridge Dilemma to indicate its immediate utility. Leveraging the centrality of perceptibility within technology governance, I deploy the sociotechnical umwelt as the outer limit of governability itself, and conclude with a plea for broadening the sociotechnical umwelt as a means of recognising latent harms.

items.title: Affect-aware human-agent conversations: towards empathic LLM interaction
items.abstract: Large Language Models can produce supportive responses, but their apparent empathic behavior is usually grounded only in explicit textual input. This paper presents Empathic Extended Prompting a real-time affect-aware framework that enriches human--LLM conversation with facial affective descriptors to support perceived empathic attunement. The system integrates FaceReader-based affective descriptors into the LLM context, including emotional intensity, valence, and arousal. We evaluated the approach in a within-subjects study with N=20 participants, comparing an affect-aware experimental condition with an empathic text-only baseline. Results favored the affect-aware condition on key perceived qualities of the interaction, particularly emotional intelligence and mood responsiveness. These findings suggest that real-time affective context may add relational grounding to LLM conversations without reducing usability or eliciting uncanny-like perceptions.

items.title: Agent Trajectories as Evidence for Software Quality Assurance
items.abstract: Autonomous software agents increasingly plan, implement, and test software with limited human oversight. Their decisions may introduce implicit assumptions that final code and passing tests do not adequately expose. We propose analyzing observable agent trajectories alongside software and agent specifications and AI generated artifacts as evidence for targeted quality assurance. The aim is to prioritize consequential decisions for scrutiny, investigate their possible contribution to software problems, and inform improvements to specifications and development practices. Industrial experience motivates the idea; available execution records and preliminary analysis methods make it plausible. However, trajectories alone do not establish that decisions are justified, outcomes acceptable, or corrective changes effective. We ask how this evidence can support review, diagnosis, and continuous quality improvement, and when simpler QA approaches suffice. Perspectives from requirements engineering, verification and validation, agent systems, causal inference, empirical software engineering, and human factors could help develop and evaluate the idea.
